To: #maintenance
Replying to: [s03]
Cc: @dana.okoye
Subject: Re: Winterizing the 3GM30F — order of operations

Dana — you're new to diesels but you're a quick study, and this is a two-afternoon job, not a mystery. One correction before you buy anything, so the weekend doesn't cost you an impeller.

Hector, no offense meant, but the green automotive antifreeze is the wrong product for a boat. That's ethylene glycol: toxic, not rated for the raw water system, and it will crack the exhaust elbow coming out of the block. Sea Wren wants pink propylene glycol RV/marine antifreeze, about $6 a gallon at West Marine or Walmart. Either color has to stay out of the river. Figure roughly 2 gallons for the engine and 2 to 3 for the water system — those are estimates only, so buy enough to finish the manufacturer's winterizing procedures, and don't judge protection by color alone.

The 3GM30F is freshwater cooled through a heat exchanger, so there are two sides. The coolant side you leave alone: pull a sample, check it with a hydrometer, and 50/50 is good down to about -20F. The raw water side is the one that freezes and cracks things.

Order:

1. Warm engine first. Oil and filter while it's warm, top off the fuel tank, add stabilizer, run it about 10 minutes to get the additive through.
2. Set up collection before you start. Raw water discharge comes out the exhaust, and the water system discharge needs catching too. Nothing goes overboard.
3. Raw water flush: seacock closed, antifreeze feeding through the strainer at idle. Keep the pump wet, don't run it dry. Shut down when it comes out pink, and leave the seacock closed.
4. Water heater: on that Catalina the bypass valve is behind the companionway steps. Switch off the water-heater breaker before you drain and leave it off until it's refilled in spring. Drain the tank first or you'll waste six gallons of pink.

Also keep a spare impeller aboard. Pull the old one and inspect it while you're in there — just don't run the engine dry to do it.

Follow the Yanmar and antifreeze manufacturers' winterizing procedures, and check the discharged mixture for actual winter protection, not just the pink color.

$465 isn't a ripoff; that's fair for the work. But you can do this in 2 to 3 hours with a helper — ideally someone who watches the flow and the collection while you're at the helm. Worth knowing why people rush it: a few Christmases ago we had a hard freeze and three boats on C dock cracked exhaust elbows or strainers. All three had skipped or hurried the raw water side.

If you want a second set of hands, I'll come down Saturday morning. I'm around.

— Walt
